text:
U.S. immigration judges have essentially been told that they cannot grant asylum to immigrants, The New York Times reported Thursday.

In a previously unreported whistleblower letter to Congress, a military lawyer who served as a temporary immigration judge before being fired, quoted an official who’d offered a frank—and dark—description of the standard for granting asylum under the Trump administration: “Maybe if you were Jewish and escaping Nazi Germany in 1943, you should get it.”

Illegally denying immigrants their lawful pathway to citizenship is just one way that President Donald Trump transformed the country’s immigration court system into the engine of his mass deportation agenda. Since Trump reentered office, his administration has carried out an unprecedented purge of the country’s immigration judges, culling 100 judges from a body of about 750 officials, according to the Times.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has sought to replace these officials with a class of so-called “deportation judges” and has announced the appointment of 143 permanent and temporary judges, many of whom previously worked as immigration prosecutors or military lawyers. As a result, deportation rates have skyrocketed and the number of successful asylum claims has seen a precipitous drop.

An analysis by the Times found that many of the judges who were fired under the Trump administration had been appointed under Democratic administrations, and tended to approve more asylum cases than their peers. Some immigration courts, such as one in San Francisco, that were viewed as friendly to asylum claims were shuttered altogether. Judges who were fired as part of Trump’s purge approved about 46 percent of asylum claims, while those who remained approved roughly 15 percent.

By comparison, the administration’s new hires have approved roughly 6 percent, according to an analysis by the Times.

The Trump administration wanted immigration judges to act as “puppets for the administration with a singular goal of deporting as many people as possible as quickly as possible,” Shuting Chen, an immigration judge who was dismissed last November, told the Times.

The immigration judges who remain have found themselves in a precarious position. More than two dozen immigration judges who spoke with the Times said they felt pressure to go along with the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda or risk losing their jobs.

Last June, a memo from a top DHS official accused certain judges of tolerating bias so long as it was “in favor of an alien,” and warned that judges who favored one side “may be subject to corrective or disciplinary action.”

“All of us are looking over our shoulders,” said Holly D’Andrea, an immigration judge in Texas who spoke with the Times in her capacity as president of the National Association of Immigration Judges union.

When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described a deadly Iranian strike in Kuwait as a rare “squirter” that had broken through the defenses of a U.S. military base, it didn’t quite sound right—especially to the service members who actually lived through it.

“Painting a picture that ‘one squeaked through’ is a falsehood,” one of the injured soldiers told CBS News Thursday. “I want people to know the unit … was unprepared to provide any defense for itself. It was not a fortified position.”

The injured soldier, a member of the Army’s 103rd Sustainment Command who spoke to CBS News under the condition of anonymity, highlighted the valiant efforts of his fellow service members who were left in a dangerous situation by their leadership.

“I don’t think that the security environment or any leadership decision diminishes in any way their sacrifice or their service,” the injured soldier told CBS in an interview. “Those soldiers put themselves in harm’s way and … I’m immensely proud of them, and their family should be proud of them.”

Ahead of Operation Epic Fury, U.S. troops in the Gulf region were instructed to move away from the “X,” or danger zone. But a group of soldiers were sent from Kuwait City to Port of Shuaiba, still well within striking distance for Iran. There, they would establish a makeshift portside tactical operations center in a series of small tin buildings.

“We moved closer to Iran, to a deeply unsafe area that was a known target,” another soldier told CBS News. “I don’t think there was a good reason ever articulated.”

The soldier described how the troops had been protected by only a thin layer of vertical standing blast barricades. “From a bunker standpoint, that’s about as weak as one gets,” he told CBS News. Images of the base showed that it had limited defenses against drone or missile strikes.

When asked to describe the degree of fortification at the makeshift operations center, the soldier told the outlet: “I mean, I would put it in the ‘none’ category. From a drone defense capability … none.”

This runs counter to the Pentagon’s repeated assertions that the operations center was fortified. “Every possible measure has been taken to safeguard our troops—at every level,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on X in March.

The Iranian strike on that base killed six U.S. service members, making it the deadliest Iranian strike of the first five weeks of the joint U.S.-Israeli military campaign in Iran. More than 30 military members were hospitalized, with dozens suffering from injuries, including burns, shrapnel wounds, and brain trauma.

The Defense Department did not initially release information about how many were hurt in the strike, and U.S. Central Command initially claimed that five had been seriously wounded. This isn’t the only case of the Pentagon downplaying the toll of Trump’s reckless war in Iran The government has published outdated numbers in statements on casualties, resulting in an undercount of how many troops have been wounded or killed, and a U.S. official said last week that the Pentagon appeared to be engaged in a “casualty cover-up” in Iran.

Barack Obama could be about to one-up Donald Trump yet again.

Pope Leo XIV met with Obama adviser David Axelrod Thursday morning, reported Substack journalist Christopher Hale, marking a major progression in the quest to land the 44th president a meeting with the Chicago-born pontiff.

Obama’s enthusiasm for meeting the pope was made apparent in February, when he joined Brian Tyler Cohen’s podcast for a Valentine’s Day episode.

“I’ll be honest with you, being president or even being an ex-president, I can kind of meet everybody, so I’ve met a lot of folks,” Obama said at the time. “The person who I have not yet met that I’m looking forward to meeting—and I hope I get an opportunity sometime in the future—is the new pope, who’s from Chicago, and a White Sox fan.”

Axelrod worked as Obama’s chief strategist on both of his presidential campaigns. It’s not clear what Axelrod and the pope discussed, but the shrinking degrees of separation between the global figures bodes well for Obama’s dream.

The effort to pair the two has been actively in the works since at least March, when Hale reported that the Holy See had been in communication with Obama’s team about arranging a meeting.

That could mean that Obama meets Pope Leo XIV before Trump does.

Leo became the first American-born pope on May 8, 2025, but Trump has not managed to meet him over the past year. Instead, the Vatican has shied away from the Trump administration, in no small part due to threats made by Defense Department officials who were unhappy with the pontiff’s various criticisms of Trump’s warmongering.

Days after Pope Leo XIV delivered his “State of the World” speech in January, Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby summoned Cardinal Christophe Pierre, the Vatican’s U.S. representative, to a closed-door meeting at the Pentagon. The atmosphere was anything but friendly: Pentagon officials openly threatened the religious ambassador, asserting that the Catholic Church needed to get behind the Trump administration’s global whims due to the country’s military prowess.

One U.S. official present at the meeting brought up the Avignon papacy, a period in the fourteenth century in which the French monarchy bent the Catholic Church into submission, ordering an attack on Pope Boniface VIII that led to his downfall and subsequent death, and forcing the papacy to relocate from Rome to Avignon.

The Vatican was so alarmed by the Pentagon’s warning that Pope Leo cancelled his plans to visit the U.S. later in the year, reported Hale, who noted that “many in the Vatican saw the Pentagon’s reference to an Avignon papacy as a threat to use military force against the Holy See.”

The Vatican also rejected the White House’s invitation to host the pope for America’s 250th anniversary on July 4.

President Trump issued an “ultimatum” to European countries regarding the Strait of Hormuz after meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the White House on Wednesday.

German news magazine Der Spiegel reported that Trump is expecting NATO members to help reopen the strait, which Iran closed in retaliation for the war Trump started without speaking to any of those NATO members. He’s also threatening to pull U.S. military support from any countries that don’t help reopen the strait.

Trump’s demand is equivalent to an “ultimatum,” several European diplomats told Der Spiegel.

“None of these people, including our own, very disappointing, NATO, understood anything unless they have pressure placed upon them!!!” Trump posted on Truth Social early Thursday morning, hours after his meeting with Rutte.

This isn’t the first time Trump has begged NATO to help him reestablish a status quo that he disrupted. Last month, Trump claimed that other countries—such as China—depend more on the Middle East waterway than the U.S. does, and should therefore be leading the charge in reopening the bomb-laden strait.

“I’m demanding that these countries come in and protect their own territory, because it is their territory. It’s the place from which they get their energy. And they should come and they should help us protect it,” Trump said. “Why are we maintaining the Hormuz Strait when it’s really there for China and many other countries? Why aren’t they doing it?”

It’s been less than 48 hours since the U.S. brokered a fragile, two-week ceasefire agreement with Iran, and Donald Trump is already raring for his next fight.

The president issued another violent threat against Iran Wednesday night, promising that the “shootin’ starts” if the two countries do not reach a “REAL AGREEMENT.”

“All U.S. Ships, Aircraft, and Military Personnel, with additional Ammunition, Weaponry, and anything else that is appropriate and necessary for the lethal prosecution and destruction of an already substantially degraded Enemy, will remain in place in, and around, Iran, until such time as the REAL AGREEMENT reached is fully complied with,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“If for any reason it is not, which is highly unlikely, then the ‘Shootin’ Starts,’ bigger, and better, and stronger than anyone has ever seen before.”

“It was agreed, a long time ago, and despite all of the fake rhetoric to the contrary—NO NUCLEAR WEAPONS and, the Strait of Hormuz WILL BE OPEN & SAFE,” he continued. “In the meantime our great Military is Loading Up and Resting, looking forward, actually, to its next Conquest. AMERICA IS BACK!”

Iran offered a 10-point peace plan on Monday that the White House tepidly agreed to work with, mere minutes before Trump’s deadline the following night to completely obliterate the country.

The plan includes various demands for an immediate end to the regional violence, including proposals for a permanent end to the war, guarantees that Iran and its allies would not be attacked again, and an end to Israeli strikes on Hezbollah in Lebanon.

It also seeks the lifting of all U.S. and international sanctions on Iran; the imposition of a new $2 million toll per ship through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil passageway situated between Iran and Oman; and a $1 toll per barrel of oil delivered through the waterway.

But there was an additional detail included in versions of the ceasefire arrangement distributed in Farsi—Iran’s native language—that was not included in the English edition, specifying the “acceptance of enrichment” for Iran’s nuclear program, suggesting that the country was not yet willing to let go of its plans to develop nuclear technology.

While it’s hard to see how any components of the deal offer a benefit to the U.S., the final point undermines Trump’s rationale for the war entirely: The president’s primary interest in fighting Iran was to cripple the country’s nuclear program, stripping any potential for the country to create a nuclear weapon. Failing to do so would imply that the war—which has so far cost the lives of 13 U.S. troops and billions of dollars in munitions—was a complete waste of time, even by the White House’s own metrics.

So much for Donald Trump’s “Golden Age.” It looks like America’s economic growth is officially in free fall.

Between October and December, America’s real gross domestic product fell from 4.4 percent to just 0.5 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis reported Thursday.

That figure is significantly less than the agency’s second estimate of 0.7 percent growth, reported last month.

The government reported that the economy grew 2.1 percent last year, compared to 2.8 percent in 2024 and 2.9 percent in 2023. If GDP growth is beneath 2 percent annually, that can typically be considered a recession.

The surprising economic slow-down in the fourth quarter can be attributed to the government shutdown, which cut federal spending and investment by 16.6 percent and trimmed 1.16 percent points off of growth in Q4. Consumer spending expanded at a pace of 1.89 percent, down from the previous estimate of 3.5 percent in the second quarter.

This weakened economy has set the stage for Trump’s increasingly expensive war in Iran. The president’s reckless military campaign in the Middle East has triggered significant disruptions in global commerce and sent energy prices surging.

Iran is not happy that Israel is continuing to bomb Lebanon and is warning Donald Trump to enforce what it says is “an inseparable part of the ceasefire.”

In a post on X Thursday morning, Iran’s speaker of parliament Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf posted three points emphasizing Lebanon’s importance to the ceasefire deal, noting that it was part of the first point in Iran’s 10-point plan, that mediator Pakistan “publicly and clearly stressed the Lebanon issue,” and that ceasefire violations “carry explicit costs and STRONG responses.”

“Extinguish the fire immediately,” Ghalibaf warned.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X Wednesday that “the Iran-U.S. Ceasefire terms are clear and explicit: the U.S. must choose—ceasefire or continued war via Israel. It cannot have both.”

“The world sees the massacres in Lebanon. The ball is in the U.S. court, and the world is watching whether it will act on its commitments,” Araghchi said.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian echoed Araghchi.

“Renewed aggression by the Zionist regime against Lebanon blatantly violates the initial ceasefire. Such actions signal deception and non-compliance, rendering negotiations meaningless. Our hands remain on the trigger. Iran will never forsake its Lebanese brothers and sisters,” Pezeshkian posted on X Thursday.

At least 203 people were killed in Lebanon in Israeli strikes on Wednesday, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry, with over 1,000 wounded. Strikes continued Thursday, with at least seven people killed in the southern Lebanese town of Abbassiyeh.

Meanwhile, the status of the Strait of Hormuz was unclear Thursday morning. Few ships were traversing it despite the supposed ceasefire, and Iranian officials said Wednesday that traffic was once again blocked due to the strikes on Lebanon. But U.S. and Israeli officials are claiming, contrary to Pakistan, that Lebanon wasn’t part of the ceasefire.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu posted on X in Hebrew Thursday morning that “we will continue to strike Hezbollah wherever required, until we restore full security to the residents of the north.”

Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that “if Iran wants to let this negotiation fall apart—in a conflict where they were getting hammered—over Lebanon, which has nothing to do with them and which the United States never once said was part of the ceasefire, that’s ultimately their choice. We think that would be dumb, but that’s their choice.”

So, is the ceasefire all but dead? Will the White House do anything about Israel’s continued bombing of Lebanon? If this two-week peace deal is meant to hold up, then these questions have to be answered, otherwise more civilians will die and things will only get worse.

text:
Thursday, the National Health Law Program (NHeLP) and American Oversight filed suit against the Trump administration for failing to release records related to a sweeping federal policy enabling the sharing of Medicaid enrollee data with immigration enforcement agencies.

The lawsuit comes amid a broader pattern of reported data sharing and use across the administration for immigration enforcement, including Medicaid data from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), taxpayer data from the Internal Revenue Service, and traveler data from the Transportation Security Administration. This pattern has also raised serious concerns about how the administration is handling sensitive personal information, including reported instances in which federal officials improperly disclosed confidential taxpayer data.

The lawsuit seeks to compel HHS and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to produce records that could shed light on how sensitive data is being shared with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The lawsuit centers on a series of Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests seeking information about the administration’s policies and practices governing the sharing of Medicaid data — including personal and demographic information — to immigration authorities. These requests follow public reporting revealing that federal officials have authorized new data-sharing arrangements that disrupt longstanding expectations that Medicaid information would remain confidential and not be used for immigration enforcement, raising serious legal and ethical concerns. While a number of states have challenged the data sharing in court, that litigation has not revealed the details of what the agencies are doing in the plaintiff states or elsewhere.

“Reports that CMS began sharing Medicaid data with ICE emerged last summer. Yet HHS and CMS have consistently refused to provide clarity about what data they are — and importantly — are not sharing,” said Sarah Grusin, Senior Attorney at the National Health Law Program. “The lack of transparency adds to the fear and confusion faced by immigrant families across the country who are left grappling with heartbreaking choices like skipping prenatal visits and keeping children off Medicaid in an effort to keep their families safe. These families deserve to know how their health care data is being used and our FOIA requests are aimed at bringing that clarity into the open.”

“The Trump administration is making deeply consequential decisions about the use of Americans’ sensitive personal information while refusing to explain how those decisions are made, what steps are being taken to protect this information, or what limits exist on that power,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “When the government begins using health data for immigration enforcement, it not only raises privacy concerns but risks deterring people from seeking essential medical care, forcing families to weigh whether getting care could put themselves or their loved ones at risk. That is not just a policy failure, it is a threat to public health, with real consequences for patients who may delay or forgo medical attention they need to stay healthy and safe. These policies should alarm anyone whose data is managed by CMS.The American people deserve answers about what data is being shared, who is affected, and how this administration is abusing its authority behind closed doors.”

NHeLP submitted multiple FOIA requests in 2025 and 2026 seeking records related to these data-sharing policies, including internal communications among senior officials, agreements between agencies, and requests from DHS and ICE for Medicaid enrollee data, as well as memoranda of understanding and communications regarding the permissibility of sharing such data under federal privacy laws. The requests also seek documents outlining how federal officials determine which individuals’ data may be shared, what categories of information are included, and how many individuals’ data have already been shared.

Despite granting expedited processing and fee waivers, the agencies have failed to produce the requested records or provide final determinations within the timeframe required by law, forcing NHeLP to file suit. The requested records could reveal the scope of data being shared, how federal agencies are interpreting their legal authority, and how these policies are affecting access to health care — particularly for immigrant families and mixed-status households.

title: Human rights groups warn of deepening humanitarian crisis in Lebanon following Israeli invasion
description:
Wednesday was the deadliest day in Lebanon since fighting between Israel and Hezbollah reignited last month.
Israel’s ongoing attacks in Lebanon are putting the United States and Israel’s fragile new ceasefire with Iran at risk, while exacerbating a brewing humanitarian crisis in the region.
Since Israel began its invasion of Lebanon last month, more than 1 million people have been forcibly displaced from their homes, and Israeli airstrikes continue to destroy houses, infrastructure and bridges, isolating the southern region of Lebanon and cutting off a lifeline to humanitarian aid.
Human Rights Watch researcher Ramzi Kaiss joins Here & Now‘s Indira Lakshmanan for an update on the deepening humanitarian crisis in the region.

title: In ICE custody, medical delays drive record deaths - San Francisco Chronicle
authors: St. John Barned-Smith, Ko Lyn Cheang
description:
Reporters spent six months obtaining detention data, ICE death reports, which record medical care a person received in custody, and, when available, autopsies, toxicology reports, coroner’s investigations and detailed medical records for all 48 cases.
Yet there is no indication in ICE records that he received treatment for the condition at Camp East Montana.
A nurse told him to return to his cell and to come back “if symptoms worsened,” ICE records state.
Inspectors discovered that medical staff weren’t giving new detainees health screenings, a “repeat deficiency,” and failed to test them for tuberculosis.
There were 23 medical fatalities that occurred in ICE custody in which the agency had published a legally required detainee death report, which details medical care a person received in custody.
text:
Ismael Ayala-Uribe was in agony.

The pain started soon after immigration agents seized the bespectacled 39-year-old man, who had lived in the United States since he was 5, at the Orange County car wash where he worked last August.

They took him to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, where he developed an abscess under the skin on his left buttock. It filled with pus and bacteria, rotting muscle and fat as it pushed into his pelvis and abdomen, threatening to flood his bloodstream with toxins.

Ayala-Uribe complained to medical staff about rectal pain, rating it “10 out of 10,” Immigration and Customs Enforcement records show, but documents do not indicate he was ever physically examined by staff members at Adelanto. On Sept. 18, a nurse gave him over-the-counter painkillers and fiber supplements used to relieve digestion problems, then sent him back to his cell.

Three days later, sweating and trembling, Ayala-Uribe was finally taken to a hospital. While waiting for treatment, he suffered septic shock caused by the abscess, according to a coroner’s report, and his heart stopped.

“This case is just absolute medical malpractice,” said Dr. Barbara Ogur, an associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School who reviewed his treatment records at the Chronicle’s request.

Advertisement

Ayala-Uribe is one of at least 48 people who have died in ICE custody since President Donald Trump returned to office on Jan. 20, 2025, and launched an aggressive immigration crackdown. Last year’s death toll of people in ICE custody — 33 — was the highest since the agency’s creation in 2003, federal records show.

Reporters spent six months obtaining detention data, ICE death reports, which record medical care a person received in custody, and, when available, autopsies, toxicology reports, coroner’s investigations and detailed medical records for all 48 cases.

The Chronicle analyzed 32 cases in which some revelatory documents were available, sending individual patient records to doctors with specialties related to the medical conditions cited in the detainees’ cause of death — including emergency room physicians, addiction specialists and psychiatrists. Reporters sent documents from each case to at least two doctors and relied on 14 doctors in total.

In all, at least 17 people in ICE custody died after medical staff delayed or failed to provide critical care that might have saved their lives, multiple doctors who reviewed their cases told the Chronicle. In some deaths, physicians’ opinions were not unanimous; some said they did not have enough information to make an evaluation.

In the 15 remaining cases, doctors either said that there was not enough information to comment or that the person was so medically frail that detention likely hastened their death. In one of these cases, a 75-year-old heart attack survivor, near-blind from cataracts, died from a heart attack weeks after being detained.

People routinely died in custody without ever being seen by doctors, even as they begged for help while gasping for air or hallucinating. Their life-threatening symptoms were often evaluated only by lower-level nurses, who are not trained or authorized to make diagnoses.

ICE facilities’ medical staff repeatedly failed to diagnose critical illnesses, misdiagnosed patients and did not call 911 in time for people experiencing emergencies, according to the Chronicle’s review.

One 44-year-old man died after detention staff waited more than an hour to call emergency medical transportation after witnessing him suffer a series of seizures. A 45-year-old man died from complications of AIDS after not being tested or treated for HIV for months. Two people died in cells from drug and alcohol withdrawal, despite an ICE policy requiring staff to send detainees experiencing severe withdrawal to an emergency department.

Eight men died by suicide at the facilities, including one at Stewart Detention Center in Georgia, which had been faulted for failing to complete suicide prevention training, and another who detention staff witnessed having a psychotic breakdown.

Advertisement

The Chronicle did not review cases in which people died in violent acts while in ICE custody. Two people were killed in a shooting at a Texas facility, one was shot in a skirmish with an ICE officer, another was suffocated by a guard (ICE initially claimed he had died by suicide), and one was hit by a car on a highway while fleeing from ICE officers.

ICE did not respond to repeated requests for comment or to detailed, written questions submitted for this story. The agency has said detainee health care is one of its “highest priorities,” stating that its facilities “provide comprehensive medical, dental and mental health care” and offer “the best healthcare that many aliens have received in their entire lives.”

But Dr. Amy Zeidan, an emergency physician and professor at Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta who was among those who reviewed the detainee death cases, said, “If you're not able to provide quality medical care or let people choose when they need to go to the emergency department, then I don't think you can claim to have appropriate medical care and detain people.”

Under federal law, immigration detention is not supposed to be a form of punishment. It’s a civil process, meant to ensure people show up for hearings or to protect the public from people deemed dangerous. ICE has broad power to decide who to detain, though many of those decisions have been successfully challenged in court. A majority of the people who died in ICE custody since 2025 didn’t have a violent criminal history, based on information the agency released.

Regardless, said Oscar Michelen, an attorney for a deceased detainee’s family, “When you take someone into custody, you’re responsible for their well-being. Even sentenced murderers are entitled to medical care.”

The Chronicle analysis found that the record fatalities were not solely due to the surge in people being arrested and detained by the Trump administration. The deaths have occurred at the highest rate per average daily population of people in detention since at least 2009, with the exception of 2020, when death rates soared due to COVID-19.

People are also dying in far less time at the facilities than in years past: after a median 27 days in custody in 2025, compared with 74 days from 2018 to 2024.

The federal government houses immigration detainees in a network of jails and facilities, some operated by public agencies and others by for-profit contractors. Most of the deaths occurred in facilities managed by private companies, the two largest of which are CoreCivic and Geo Group. CoreCivic posted record revenues in 2025 while Geo Group boasted of record new business as it secured federal contracts.

Health care in detention facilities is provided by these third-party contractors, ICE Health Service Corps employees, or federal or county agencies.

Just nine of the more than 220 immigration detention facilities across the country accounted for half the deaths since the beginning of 2025, the Chronicle found, despite holding no more than 16% of the national detainee population on three dates across that period. Five of these facilities were cited for medical care deficiencies after their most recent inspections by ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight. CoreCivic and Geo Group each operate two of the eight facilities.

Asked for comment, Geo Group referred the Chronicle to ICE. CoreCivic spokesperson Brian Todd declined to comment on individual deaths, citing medical privacy laws, but stated that “nothing matters more to CoreCivic than the health and safety of the people in our care” and that it provides high-quality medical and mental health care for all detainees, following company and government standards.

Information about the quality of care in ICE custody is increasingly limited. Under the Trump administration, two detention watchdog agencies have been gutted, and inspections by a third oversight body, ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight, have plummeted.

ICE detainee death reports have in the past few months become shorter and less detailed in describing the medical care a person received before they died, which doctors said made it difficult to evaluate that care. The Chronicle requested fuller records, called mortality reviews, but the agency did not respond by the legally required Freedom of Information Act deadline.

Advertisement

Michelle Brané, who was immigration detention ombudsman under President Joe Biden’s administration, when 26 people died in ICE custody over four years, said she believes that poor medical care offered at detention facilities under the Trump administration is by design.

“They want the circumstances in custody to be so bad that people take removal and give up their rights,” said Brané, who now directs Together and Free, a nonprofit organization that helps families navigate immigration enforcement.

An excruciating death

“Migra here,” Ayala-Uribe texted his sister at 9:30 a.m. on Aug. 17, referring to immigration agents. Border Patrol agents were raiding the Fountain Valley car wash where he’d worked for 15 years. Ten minutes later, his friend called to tell the family that the agents had taken him.

The oldest of three, Ayala-Uribe loved playing the role of adoring son and uncle, said his mother, Lucia Uribe-Martinez. He relished being chosen as godfather for his niece’s baptism, treating her like his own daughter.

Though he didn’t make much money, he was quick to share what he had, his mother said.

“He took care of me,” Uribe-Martinez said in Spanish. “Whatever little thing we wanted, he’d buy it for us.”

A relative had brought Ayala-Uribe to the U.S. from Mexico in 1991. Over the years, his parents and younger sister became citizens. His brother was born in the United States. Ayala-Uribe received Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals status in 2012, but lost it in 2016 after he was convicted of driving while intoxicated. In June 2019, he was convicted again for the same offense.

Five days after the raid, ICE transferred Ayala-Uribe to the Adelanto center, run by Geo Group. Ayala-Uribe had been fairly healthy, his family said, apart from high blood pressure.

Initially, Ayala-Uribe called home daily to talk to his nephews. Soon, however, his mom noticed something was wrong. First a cough, then a fever. He said he had a spot on his buttock that had started to hurt and just kept getting worse.

“He started having pains,” his brother, Jose Ayala, said, “but they really didn’t want to do anything.”

The pain grew so bad that when Ayala-Uribe visited the detention infirmary on Sept. 18, staff took him there in a wheelchair, according to ICE records. He told a nurse it was unbearable. A physician ordered pain medications, anti-inflammatory ointment, a fiber supplement and twice-daily wellness checks for 10 days.

When Uribe-Martinez made the two-hour drive to see her son on Sept. 20, she was shocked by how sick and pale he looked.

“Don’t stress,” she told him. “Be calm.”

Hours later, Ayala-Uribe returned to the infirmary vomiting, records show. Staff sent him to a local hospital, where doctors found the abscess and a serious blood infection. They considered surgery — but before they took action, he stopped breathing.

In a press release after he died, ICE said, “At no time during detention is a detained illegal alien denied emergent care.”

Geo Group declined to comment on Ayala-Uribe’s case, referring the Chronicle to ICE, which did not respond to detailed questions about the death.

Five doctors who reviewed Ayala-Uribe’s case said he could have survived if a physician had examined him earlier, because they would have diagnosed and drained the abscess and treated the infection.

“This was a young man who never should have died,” said Dr. William Weber, a Minneapolis-based emergency physician and medical director of the prison health care advocacy nonprofit Medical Justice Alliance who reviewed Ayala-Uribe’s case.

Instead, Dr. Weber said, he suffered “an excruciating death, in an unfamiliar location, away from his family, after he’d tried as hard as he could to get support from people constitutionally required to care for him.”

Missed diagnoses, deadly delays

Physicians who reviewed the records of immigration detainee deaths since Trump’s inauguration identified at least 13 people who died after medical staff misdiagnosed or failed to evaluate and diagnose them for conditions that later killed them.

Francisco Gaspar-Andrés, a 48-year-old Guatemalan man with no criminal history, was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis at a hospital days after he was arrested in Florida in September. But when he was transferred to Camp East Montana in Texas days later, detention staff noted that he had “no significant medical history,” according to ICE’s detainee death report.

Over the next two months, he went to the medical unit nine times, complaining of symptoms including bloody stool and bleeding gums that, according to four doctors that reviewed his case, likely resulted from severe liver deterioration.

Yet there is no indication in ICE records that he received treatment for the condition at Camp East Montana. He was sent back from visits to the medical unit with allergy, heartburn and indigestion medications and diagnosed with influenza despite repeatedly testing negative.

The facility operator, Acquisition Logistics, did not respond to a request for comment. The Virginia-based company had no experience in detention management when it was awarded the $1.2 billion contract last year.

At ICE’s first and only inspection of the facility in February, inspectors found 49 deficiencies, including a failure to isolate or notify ICE of detainees with tuberculosis symptoms, a failure to test them for HIV, a lack of appropriate sexual abuse and assault response policies, and a failure to respond to detainee complaints about medical care promptly. Though required to respond within five business days, staff members responded to complaints in six to 14 business days in a number of cases, inspectors found.

Inspectors graded the facility as “acceptable,” the lowest passing rating. ICE has very rarely failed facilities in inspections.

When Gaspar-Andrés was finally sent to a hospital in November, he had liver failure. He died from the condition two weeks later. All four doctors who reviewed his case said they thought he could have survived if he’d been treated for liver disease earlier.

“This person is telling you they’re dying for two months, and you ignored it,” said Dr. Zeidan, the Emory professor and physician.

In many cases, immigration detainees died after receiving either delayed care or no treatment after detention staff learned of their medical conditions, or after they complained to staff about symptoms of a condition that then killed them, physicians told the Chronicle.

Luis Beltran Yanez Cruz, a 68-year-old Honduran construction worker, had just finished breakfast at a New Jersey McDonald’s when he was arrested in an ICE operation alongside other day laborers.

He’d come to the U.S. illegally 26 years earlier, and had no criminal history. A father of three, he adored his six grandchildren, whom he affectionately called his “cocolitos,” his daughter Josselyn Yanez said.

Days after being transferred to Imperial Regional Detention Center, run by Management and Training Corp. in the California border city of Calexico in late November, Cruz began experiencing stomach pain, acid reflux and shortness of breath. He sought medical attention over several weeks, ICE records show, “receiving symptomatic treatment and dietary advice from nursing staff.”

Three doctors who reviewed his case said that his symptoms signaled early stages of a heart attack or an impending heart attack and that he should have been sent to an emergency room for treatment.

When he called his daughter, he told her he felt like he was suffocating and was vomiting up his meals.

On Jan. 4, he visited the detention medical clinic again complaining of chest pain. A nurse told him to return to his cell and to come back “if symptoms worsened,” ICE records state.

That night, as Cruz’s condition deteriorated, he was finally transferred to a hospital. By then, he was critically ill from an untreated, massive heart attack and congestive heart failure. He died two days later.

Three physician reviewers said that if not for the delayed care, his death could have been prevented.

“I would call that very poor care, and it strongly appears to be negligent care,” said Dr. David Baron, a Cambridge, Mass.-based internal medicine physician of 35 years. Registered nurses are not qualified to evaluate or give medical advice on life-threatening symptoms like chest pain, Baron said, and should have escalated his case to a doctor.

“Either their policies and practices are not to refer life-threatening symptoms to a doctor, or they’re just frankly incompetent.”

Emily Lawhead, a spokesperson for Management and Training Corp., said Cruz was “treated quickly and promptly by medical staff before being sent to the hospital for further, more comprehensive care.” Complaints of chest pain are taken seriously, she said, and “outside commentators do not have access to complete medical records.”

Yanez told her son that Grandpa had gone to heaven. His body was sent to his brothers in Honduras to be buried.

“What hurts the most is that they didn’t help my dad,” Yanez said in Spanish. “And knowing that he died alone, without family.”

Ignored guidelines, missed emergencies

Three people who died of alcohol or drug withdrawal could have survived if they had received appropriate, timely treatment, two addiction medicine specialists said. In each case, detention staff appeared to violate ICE standards that require detainees experiencing “severe, life-threatening” alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms to be transferred “immediately” to an emergency department.

Only one of the three, Gabriel Garcia Aviles, was ever transferred to a hospital. Even then, staff took six hours to do so.

Aviles, a 54-year-old day laborer from Mexico who loved riding his bicycle with his children, died in October, nine days after being detained at the Adelanto center while suffering alcohol withdrawal.

“He never committed any big crime or anything like that,” said Aviles’ son, Gabriel Alejandro Garcia. “I think his crime was just to cross over here for his kids and give us a better life.”

Shortly after ICE arrested Santos Banegas Reyes, a 42-year-old Honduran father working as a day laborer in New York on Sept. 17, 2025, he was trembling and suffering from abdominal pain. He told a nurse he drank daily. A doctor diagnosed him with alcohol withdrawal and sent him to his cell with a “low bunk pass for seizure precautions.”

ICE records do not provide any indication that staff checked on him over the next 17 hours. By the time a detention officer found Reyes the next morning, his body was cold. ICE records listed the preliminary cause of death as apparent “liver failure complicated by alcoholism.”

Dr. Jose Luis Gonzalez, an addiction medicine specialist, said that someone should have been evaluating Reyes every two hours if he had severe alcohol withdrawal. With careful monitoring and treatment, alcohol withdrawal is survivable, he said.

“How was it that he was just found unresponsive?” he said. “It’s almost 24 hours, 17 hours, presumably, with no vital signs.”

The third man, Parady La, was a 46-year-old Cambodian refugee. His 23-year-old daughter remembered him for his love of tennis, which he taught her to play. He was diagnosed with severe opiate withdrawal soon after being detained and was found unresponsive, in critical condition, in a cell at Federal Detention Center in Philadelphia.

Federal Bureau of Prisons spokesperson Emery Nelson declined to comment on La’s case, but said that it provides “urgent and emergent evaluations when needed.”

Dr. Ryan Marino, an emergency medicine and addiction medicine physician and an assistant professor at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, said that if the three men received proper medical care, “all those people should be alive, based on the information DHS put out.”

At least 10 people died after staff members at detention centers did not call 911 or send patients to an emergency room in situations that doctors who reviewed their cases said should have warranted a more urgent response.

Lorenzo Antonio Batrez Vargas, 32, was living in Arizona, taking care of his mom as she battled cancer, when he was arrested by local police on suspicion of drug possession in August. ICE picked him up from Coconino County Jail and placed him in removal proceedings.

In custody at a Central Arizona detention facility run by CoreCivic, he contracted COVID-19. He recovered but soon complained to a facility nurse of dizziness and difficulty breathing, and he had an abnormally fast heart rate. An advanced practice provider, a lower-level medical provider than a licensed doctor, sent him back to detention with a fever reducer, decongestant medication and an inhaler.

He returned the next day, Aug. 31, 2025, still struggling to breathe and with shoulder pain. Three doctors who reviewed his case said he should have been sent to an emergency room. Instead, a nurse “advised him to notify medical staff of any changes to his condition,” records show.

An hour later, he was dead. His cause of death was acute bronchopneumonia from influenza, according to the coroner’s report.

“It’s as if you see someone floundering and drowning,” said Dr. Weber, the Minneapolis emergency physician, “and you say, ‘OK, well just let me know if anything changes,’ and you wait until they go under and they’re drowned.”

Maksym Chernyak, 44, had fled to the U.S. in August 2024, leaving his home country of Ukraine and the war that had consumed it. He and his girlfriend, Oksana Tarasiuk, were granted humanitarian parole under the Biden-era Uniting for Ukraine program and hoped to make a new start in Miami.

Instead, in January 2025, neighbors called the police when they overheard the couple arguing. Neither Chernyak nor Tarasiuk spoke English. In the subsequent misunderstanding, Tarasiuk said, police arrested Chernyak.

Tarasiuk, who’d met Chernyak at a restaurant near Kiev in 2021, said it was love at first sight. After her boyfriend’s arrest, she posted his bail. But ICE agents lodged a detainment request and Broward County deputies took Chernyak to Krome Detention Center, run by Akima Global Services LLC, on Miami’s western outskirts. Akima did not respond to a request for comment.

Tarasiuk said Chernyak soon called her from the lockup and told her that he was being kept in frigid conditions and forced to sleep on concrete — and that he started getting sick.

During three medical appointments, detention staff found Chernyak had high blood pressure, according to records provided to the Chronicle by his attorney. Those levels, if sustained, can put someone at increased risk of a stroke, said neurologist Dr. Laura Boylan, who served as a New York University School of Medicine adjunct professor for 25 years.

However, medical records show Chernyak received no blood pressure treatment. ICE records referred to “slightly elevated blood pressure.”

The couple usually spoke by phone in the afternoon, Tarasiuk said. But one day, she didn’t hear from him. That night, around 2:30 a.m. on Feb. 18, 2025, detention staff witnessed Chernyak having a seizure, vomiting and passing out.

A detention nurse took him to the facility’s clinic. Records show that the nurse practitioner on call thought he was intoxicated and called for nonemergency medical transportation to a hospital. Staff tried to put him in a wheelchair, but he slid out. Over the next hour and 13 minutes, staff members witnessed him suffering six more seizures before they finally called 911, according to ICE records.

By the time he was evaluated at the hospital two hours after his first seizure, he was comatose. Doctors diagnosed the episode as a massive stroke caused by uncontrolled high blood pressure and said he had “irreversible brain damage,” according to his hospital records. He died two days later.

“That was clearly inappropriate triage,” said Dr. Elizabeth Burner, a University of Southern California associate professor and emergency physician. “A seizure is an immediately life-threatening event, especially a first-time seizure.”

Four doctors who evaluated the available records from his case said Chernyak’s death could have been prevented if 911 had been called after the first seizure and three doctors said his high blood pressure increased his risk of stroke.

Four deaths since Trump returned to office occurred at Krome, which ICE inspectors faulted in 2025 for a shortage of medical staff and overcrowding. Inspectors discovered that medical staff weren’t giving new detainees health screenings, a “repeat deficiency,” and failed to test them for tuberculosis.

While doctors unsuccessfully tried to save Chernyak, Tarasiuk was begging hospital staff to let her see him. They refused, citing that he was in ICE custody. On Feb. 20, 2025 she drove to her attorney’s office to pay for Chernyak’s deportation legal defense. Her lawyer walked over to her and whispered in her ear — her partner was dead.

Tarasiuk plans to return to Europe in a few months and scatter his ashes in the Alps, the mountains where he loved to hike and ski. The experience has changed her opinion of the United States, she said.

“We heard that the United States respects the human rights and freedom of people who live in it,” Tarasiuk said in Ukrainian. “So we hoped that we would be able to start our new stable life without war. Now I have a fear of being here in this country as well.”

Self-harm and frailty

Two psychiatrists said that of the eight people who died by suicide in ICE detention, they were most troubled by the case of Leo Cruz Silva, a 34-year-old Mexican man arrested in Missouri in September 2025 on suspicion of public intoxication.

From the moment an ICE officer detained him at a county jailhouse, records show, officials knew he was paranoid and hearing voices. The next day, a nurse saw him “hiding under his bed” and reported he was experiencing “audio and visual hallucinations.”

Dr. Joanne Ahola, a psychiatrist and medical director emeritus of the Weill Cornell Center for Human Rights, said the symptoms pointed to an acute psychotic crisis or acute delirium, which was “as much of an emergency as a heart attack,” requiring a 911 call and close monitoring for suicidality.

Instead, staff members kept Cruz Silva in his detention cell, prescribed antipsychotic medication and planned to evaluate him “the following week.”

The next day, staff found him dead in his cell. He had hanged himself. Dr. Jacob M. Appel, an emergency room psychiatrist at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York, said Cruz Silva’s treatment “defies any reasonable standard.” Suicides in ICE detention, he said, can be prevented with better screening, monitoring and “suicide-proofing” facilities such as by ensuring nothing can be hung from ceilings.

Isidro Perez was a 75-year-old grandfather who fled to Florida from Cuba when he was 16 and was granted entry to the U.S. He was convicted of two drug possession charges in the early 1980s, and sentenced to a total of 28 months in prison. It’s not clear what his immigration status was at the time.

After his release, he continued living in the U.S., working as a mechanic and fisherman and living on a boat, said his former partner, Maria Alaniz, 83.

He developed coronary heart disease and had stents placed in his heart. Then in June 2025, ICE officers arrested him, asserting he was present without admission or parole. He couldn’t see well due to cataracts and needed help getting in and out of his boat, Alaniz said. He’d also recently broken his shoulder in a fall, she said.

Perez called and told her that there were no beds for him to sleep on at the detention center and that the facility was kept at a frigid temperature. As the days passed, Perez reported in his calls that he was suffering from increasing pain, she said. “I can’t take it anymore,” she recalled him saying.

Perez died of a heart attack three weeks after being detained.

“The way they kept him wasn’t right,” Alaniz said. “It wasn’t humane. It was very hard.”

Two doctors who reviewed his case questioned why ICE detained him, given his poor health.

“You have a frail elderly man,” said Dr. Baron. “Putting him in a stressful environment, you put him at greater risk of a heart attack.”

Questionable care preceded Trump

Two of the 48 people who died in immigration detention since last year passed away just days after President Trump took office, following care they received under the Biden administration.

One was Serawit Gezahegn Dejene, a 45-year-old Ethiopian man who was arrested near the U.S.-Mexico border in August 2024. He was taken to Eloy Detention Center in Arizona, run by CoreCivic, which since 2004 has the highest number of fatalities of any immigration detention center.

During his intake screening at Eloy, a nurse wrote that Dejene denied having a history of any medical conditions. But over four months, he lost 20% of his body weight, complained to medical staff four times of back pain, had an elevated heart rate and was diagnosed with lymphoma.

Three doctors who reviewed his case said those symptoms should have prompted staff to test him for HIV. If they had, they could have started Dejene on antiretroviral therapy, likely prolonging his life.

It wasn’t until after he was transferred to a hospital intensive care unit at Banner-University Medical Center in Phoenix on Dec. 31, 2024, that physicians identified Dejene’s “immunocompromised status,” records show. Dejene was HIV-positive.

Doctors at the hospital found he had pneumonia, sepsis and lymphoma that had spread to his lungs, and had suffered a stroke. They removed him from life support on Jan. 29, 2025, according to ICE records. He died hours later, 9 days into Trump’s new term.

Physicians questioned why it took so long to determine Dejene had HIV, when testing adults for sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV, is standard medical practice.

“He never should have reached this stage,” said Dr. Salim S. Abdool Karim, a Columbia University professor and the director of the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa. “He died of multiple opportunistic infections. The sad part is all of them are eminently preventable with timely AIDS treatment.”

Even survivors struggled

Across the country and beyond, detainees, their families and advocates are seeking reforms for what they argue are broad failures of health care in immigration lockups.

Detainees have sued ICE multiple times, including in a January lawsuit seeking class action status over conditions in Adelanto, where four people have died in custody under the Trump administration. Plaintiffs alleged they were denied medication and subjected to mold infestation and outbreaks of chickenpox and staph infection.

ICE has argued in legal filings that plaintiffs did not show “irreparable harm” and rebutted their legal grounds for suing.

Officials from Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement March 30 calling for an investigation into conditions at the facility “due to grave omissions and evident deficiencies in medical care provided to detainees.”

At the national level, California Sen. Alex Padilla is co-sponsoring a bill seeking to improve the conditions and oversight of ICE detention centers. “It’s unthinkable that people are dying from preventable causes while in federal custody in the United States, but that’s the cruel reality of Donald Trump’s America,” Padilla said.

In California, immigrants at the state’s largest ICE detention center, in Kern County, sued the government over delayed medical treatment in November, prompting a federal judge to install an independent medical monitor.

Masuma Khan, 64, who was detained at the California City facility the previous month, is now working with state lawmakers on a bill to fine private operators up to $25,000 per day for violations of an array of health, safety and labor standards.

Khan, who is fighting deportation, said in an interview that she requested blood pressure medication, asthma inhalers and medicated eye drops after being detained. But she didn’t receive them for six days, medical records show. She didn’t get pills to manage her asthma until 28 days into detention.

Khan’s daughter, Riya, visited her six days in and said Khan struggled to breathe and speak and had bruised, swollen legs. Based on the blood pressure reading Khan saw when a nurse took it, she was bordering on a hypertensive crisis and at risk of a stroke, a doctor who reviewed her case at the Chronicle’s request said.

She and her daughter said they complained until Khan finally received some of her medication. Khan, who was soon ordered released by a federal judge who said her detention was illegal, said in an interview, “I was putting sick calls two, three times every day, asking them for my medicine. They didn’t care.”

The spokesperson for CoreCivic, which operates the facility, declined to comment on Khan’s case, citing medical privacy, but said detainees have access to a “continuum of health care services,” including a pharmacy.

Since Ayala-Uribe’s death, his family’s home in Huntington Beach has felt empty, Jose Ayala said. In the bedroom the brothers once shared, their mother placed a candle and photo of Ismael close to his former bedside. Every Sunday, the family drives to the cemetery to visit his grave.

His father and mother can’t speak about Ismael’s death without choking up.

The family filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Adelanto operator Geo Group, which did not respond to questions about the litigation. The suit, filed Dec. 31, argues that Ayala-Uribe’s death was due to “deliberate indifference” to the poor conditions at the facility and the “callous disregard” for his rights.

“I want justice,” his mother said. “They’re not animals. … This was a sin.”

About this story

The Chronicle focused reporting on 32 detainee death cases in which some revelatory documents were available.

Reporters then asked 14 doctors with specialties relevant to the detainees’ causes of death — including emergency room physicians, addiction specialists and psychiatrists — to review ICE death reports and, when available, autopsies, toxicology reports, coroner’s investigations and medical records for these cases. These documents were either obtained by the Chronicle through records requests, were publicly available, or were provided by families or attorneys.

The doctors practice all over the U.S. Some previously conducted research into health care in immigration detention settings, or advocated for higher-quality care.

At least two physicians and as many as five reviewed each of the cases. There were 23 medical fatalities that occurred in ICE custody in which the agency had published a legally required detainee death report, which details medical care a person received in custody. Doctors also reviewed one drug withdrawal death in which the report had not been published. Two psychiatrists reviewed each of the eight suicides in ICE custody.

In each case, the Chronicle asked doctors whether the person did not receive appropriate and timely medical treatment that could have saved the person’s life.

The Chronicle then conducted further reporting on 17 cases in which at least two doctors said medical staff delayed or failed to provide this potentially lifesaving care. In these cases, the physicians’ opinions were not necessarily unanimous. Some said they did not have enough information to make an evaluation, which the Chronicle indicated in its database.

The Chronicle did not ask doctors to review five deaths from fatal violence, nor deaths that occurred outside a detention facility though in ICE custody.
